title: SYNDACTYLY, TYPE III
alt_titles: SYNDACTYLY OF FINGERS IV AND V

intro.text: This entry describes type III syndactyly (SDTY3), syndactyly of the ring and little fingers, which has been reported as an isolated autosomal dominant trait and in families with features of oculodentodigital dysplasia.

checks.claim: Type III syndactyly (SDTY3) is syndactyly of the ring and little fingers.
checks.evidence_quote: familial syndactyly of the ring and little finger (Type III syndactyly)
checks.explanation: The abstract defines type III syndactyly as syndactyly of the ring and little finger.

checks.claim: Type III syndactyly has been reported as an isolated autosomal dominant trait.
checks.evidence_quote: Five new cases of isolated syndactyly of the small and ring finger are described. Autosomal dominant inheritance is obvious.
checks.explanation: The paper reports isolated cases with autosomal dominant inheritance.

checks.claim: Type III syndactyly has been reported in families with features of oculodentodigital dysplasia.
checks.evidence_quote: A family is described with type III syndactyly and facies resembling the oculodentodigital dysplasia facial phenotype in the absence of any of the other characteristic findings of the latter condition.
checks.explanation: The paper reports a family with type III syndactyly and ODDD-like facial features. Facial appearance was the only ODDD feature present.

paragraphs.text: Type III syndactyly is fusion of the ring and little fingers (McKiernan and McCann, 1993; De Smet et al., 1994). It can occur as an isolated trait with autosomal dominant inheritance, and brachymesophalangia of the fifth finger is a frequent association (De Smet et al., 1994). Type III syndactyly also occurs as part of oculodentodigital syndrome (Gladwin et al., 1997), and whether the two conditions are separate entities or form a clinical spectrum has been debated (Brueton et al., 1990; Schrander-Stumpel et al., 1993).

checks.claim: Type III syndactyly is fusion of the ring and little fingers.
checks.evidence_quote: Five new cases of isolated syndactyly of the small and ring finger are described.
checks.explanation: Syndactyly of the ring and small fingers is the fusion the claim describes.

checks.claim: Type III syndactyly can occur as an isolated trait with autosomal dominant inheritance.
checks.evidence_quote: Five new cases of isolated syndactyly of the small and ring finger are described. Autosomal dominant inheritance is obvious.
checks.explanation: The abstract states that the trait is isolated and inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.

checks.evidence_quote: Oculodentodigital dysplasia and type III syndactyly: separate genetic entities or disease spectrum?
checks.explanation: The title asks exactly this question, and the abstract says the relationship between the two conditions is discussed.

paragraphs.text: Opjordsmoen and Nyberg-Hansen (1980) reported a family from northern Norway in which 9 of 22 members across 3 generations had spastic paraplegia with neurogenic bladder disturbances (uninhibited, incomplete supranuclear bladder paresis) and syndactyly. The bladder disturbances were the main complaint and appeared early in the disease. The authors considered the family probably to represent an unusual form of hereditary spastic paraplegia with autosomal dominant inheritance.

checks.evidence_quote: a family settled in the northern part of Norway, with a hereditary neurological disorder consisting clinically of spastic paraplegia associated with neurogenic bladder disturbances and syndactylia. Nine out of 22 members in three generations exhibit these clinical features.
checks.explanation: The abstract gives the family's location, the 9 of 22 count and all three features.

checks.explanation: The abstract describes the bladder problem as an incomplete supranuclear bladder paresis, which it calls an uninhibited neurogenic bladder.

checks.evidence_quote: The family probably represents an unusual form of hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP). The mode of inheritance is considered to be autosomal dominant.
checks.explanation: The abstract states both points: probably an unusual form of HSP, and autosomal dominant inheritance.

They discussed whether the two conditions are separate genetic entities or part of a disease spectrum.

paragraphs.text: Schrander-Stumpel et al. (1993) reported a newborn male with complete cutaneous syndactyly of fingers 3-5 in the left hand and fingers 4-5 in the right hand. His mother and maternal grandmother were born with the same hand malformation. The mother had a thin nose and small teeth, and the grandmother had had very small teeth with enamel hypoplasia; eyes were normal in both. The authors concluded that the family showed the variable expression of oculodentodigital dysplasia and proposed that type III syndactyly and oculodentodigital dysplasia form a clinical spectrum.

paragraphs.text: Autosomal dominant inheritance of type III syndactyly was observed across 3 generations in the family reported by Schrander-Stumpel et al. (1993). McKiernan and McCann (1993) stated that analysis of their pedigree with 14 affected individuals confirmed autosomal dominant inheritance, and De Smet et al. (1994) stated that autosomal dominant inheritance was obvious in their cases of isolated ring and small finger syndactyly. Opjordsmoen and Nyberg-Hansen (1980) considered the inheritance of spastic paraplegia, neurogenic bladder and syndactyly in their Norwegian family to be autosomal dominant.

checks.claim: Autosomal dominant inheritance of type III syndactyly was observed across 3 generations in the family reported by Schrander-Stumpel et al. (1993).
checks.evidence_quote: The mother and maternal grandmother were born with the same hand malformation.
checks.explanation: Three affected generations (grandmother, mother, son) are described, and the abstract states "Inheritance is autosomal dominant."

checks.claim: McKiernan and McCann (1993) stated that analysis of their pedigree with 14 individuals affected by ring and little finger syndactyly confirmed autosomal dominant inheritance.
checks.evidence_quote: We present a pedigree containing 14 cases of familial syndactyly of the ring and little finger (Type III syndactyly).
checks.explanation: The abstract states that the pedigree contains 14 cases. The next sentence adds: 'Analysis of the pedigree confirms the autosomal dominant nature of the genetic defect.'

checks.claim: De Smet et al. (1994) stated that autosomal dominant inheritance was obvious in their cases of isolated ring and small finger syndactyly.
checks.evidence_quote: Autosomal dominant inheritance is obvious.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.claim: Opjordsmoen and Nyberg-Hansen (1980) considered the inheritance of spastic paraplegia, neurogenic bladder and syndactyly in their Norwegian family to be autosomal dominant.
checks.evidence_quote: The mode of inheritance is considered to be autosomal dominant.
checks.explanation: The authors considered the disorder in this family, which includes all three features, to be autosomal dominant.

paragraphs.text: Gladwin et al. (1997) analyzed a large family with type III syndactyly and atypical facial features. Their analysis suggested that isolated type III syndactyly maps to the same region of chromosome 6q (6q22-q24) as the oculodentodigital syndrome locus.

checks.claim: Gladwin et al. (1997) analyzed a large family with type III syndactyly and atypical facial features.
checks.evidence_quote: Analysis of a large family with type III syndactyly, but atypical facial features, further suggested that isolated type III syndactyly is also located in this same region of the genome.
checks.explanation: The abstract describes the analysis of this family.

checks.claim: The analysis by Gladwin et al. (1997) suggested that isolated type III syndactyly maps to chromosome 6q22-q24.
checks.evidence_quote: further suggested that isolated type III syndactyly is also located in this same region of the genome.
checks.explanation: The region is the ODD region on 6q, given in the title as 6q22-q24.

checks.claim: The analysis by Gladwin et al. (1997) suggested that the isolated type III syndactyly locus maps to the same region of chromosome 6q as the oculodentodigital syndrome locus.
checks.evidence_quote: further suggested that isolated type III syndactyly is also located in this same region of the genome.
checks.explanation: The abstract places it in the same region as the ODD locus.

paragraphs.text: Paznekas et al. (2003) found mutations in the GJA1 gene, which encodes connexin-43, in all 17 families with autosomal dominant oculodentodigital dysplasia that they screened. They detected 16 different missense mutations and 1 codon duplication, and noted that type III syndactyly can occur in some cases of that syndrome.

checks.evidence_quote: The human connexin 43 gene, or GJA1, is located at human chromosome 6q22-q23
checks.explanation: The abstract names GJA1 as the connexin 43 gene.

checks.claim: Paznekas et al. (2003) screened 17 families with autosomal dominant oculodentodigital dysplasia.
checks.evidence_quote: We found mutations in the GJA1 gene in all 17 families with oculodentodigital dysplasia that we screened.
checks.explanation: The abstract reports 17 families screened, and elsewhere calls the syndrome autosomal dominant.
